design_detail: Qualitative story-completion study (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, online first 10 October 2025, article pages 1-11; received 30 January, revised 9 July, accepted 30 July 2025). Not a commentary: 30 veterans with a previous PTSD diagnosis receiving care at one VA hospital in the north-eastern United States listened to a vignette about 'Chris', a combat veteran whose doctor offers him a clinical trial of MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT), and completed the story aloud in answer to five open prompts (reaction, prior knowledge, questions and concerns, hopes, decision; Appendix, p. 11). Recordings were transcribed and coded by three authors (43 codes); coders also rated each participant's willingness and familiarity on 0-100 scales; codes were correlated (Kendall's tau) with demographics, story length, drug use, PCL-5 and PHQ-9. Table 1 (code definitions, examples, frequencies) and Table 2 (correlations above |0.30|). The Introduction and Discussion contain background statements about the phase 3 trials and the 2024 FDA decision, taken from other sources, which this card records separately.
can_establish: Which questions, hopes and concerns these 30 veterans voiced, as coded by the authors, when asked to imagine a fellow veteran being offered MDMA-assisted therapy in a trial.
cannot_establish: How common any of these attitudes is among veterans with PTSD, what the participants themselves would decide, or anything about the efficacy, blinding or safety of MDMA-assisted therapy: the statements about the trials and the FDA are background from other sources (news reports for the FDA) or unreferenced.

sample.recruitment: Veteran patients of one VA hospital in the north-eastern United States (the procedures were approved by the IRB of the Stratton VA Medical Center, Albany). How participants were identified, approached and selected, how many declined, and whether they were paid are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All 30 reported a previous diagnosis of, and treatment for, PTSD; no other criteria are reported.
sample.demographics: Ages 30-77 (mean 51.03, SD 14.49). Education: some college 14 (46.7%), college graduate 10 (33.3%), graduate degree 4 (13.3%), some high school 1 (3.3%), high school diploma or equivalent 1 (3.3%). PCL-5 19-65 (mean 43.67, SD 10.91); PHQ-9 8-21 (mean 14.70, SD 3.74). Lifetime use of 1 to 8 of 11 listed substance classes (mean 3.37, SD 2.19), past-year use 0 to 7 (mean 1.57); lifetime use of 0 to 3 of four psychedelics listed (MDMA, LSD, ketamine, psilocybin; mean 0.77), past-year 0 to 3 (mean 0.23).
sample.selection_effects: One site; recruitment not described; 29 of 30 White and 25 of 30 men. The authors note that more articulate or temperamentally open veterans may be overrepresented and that one BIPOC participant limits generalizability. Saturation is asserted from the sample size (9-17 interviews usually suffice) rather than assessed in these data.

exposure.measurement: Self-report: yes/no lifetime and past-year use of alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, amphetamine, MDMA, LSD, ketamine, opiates, sedatives, inhalants and psilocybin; summed as counts. No quantities or frequencies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the participants. The vignette (Appendix) describes the treatment as several preparatory meetings with the people who would sit with the patient during the drug's effects, three sessions with MDMA, and later sessions to discuss the experience; no doses are given.
exposure.polysubstance: Counts of substances ever used and used in the past year were used as correlates of the codes.

comparison.controls: None (qualitative design). Comparisons are correlations between codes and participant characteristics.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Participants' own prior knowledge of MDMA-AT was not asked; 'familiarity' was rated by coders from the transcripts.

outcomes.instruments: Story-completion vignette with five open prompts (Appendix); PCL-5 (Cronbach's alpha 0.86, McDonald's omega 0.85); PHQ-9 (alpha 0.53, omega indeterminate); 43 codes generated top-down from the prompts and bottom-up from the responses and defined in Table 1; coder-rated willingness and familiarity (0-100).
outcomes.validity_norms: Inter-rater agreement: Cohen's kappa 0.65 to 1.00 across codes, with four codes below conventional reliability (reported anyway); Kendall's tau between raters 0.76 (familiarity) and 0.77 (willingness).
outcomes.operationalization: A theme is a code present in at least 3 of the 30 stories (27 themes). 'Wrong information' is a statement about MDMA treatment given as fact that the coders judged clearly incorrect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Codes were correlated with willingness, familiarity, story length, lifetime and past-year drug use, PCL-5, PHQ-9 and demographic variables; 'given the number of analyses' only Kendall's tau values above |0.30| are reported, without p-values. n_outcomes_tested counts the codes defined.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable in the usual sense; the coders were authors who also generated the codes, and the interviewer (CH) helped generate the initial codes. No blinding of coders to participant characteristics is reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive frequencies (Table 1) and Kendall's tau values (Table 2) without p-values or intervals; for example willingness with familiarity 0.431, willingness with the code 'Skeptical' -0.699, story length with asking about booster sessions 0.499.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or published protocol is mentioned; IRB approval at the Stratton VA Medical Center.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 lists 27 themes and the two ratings although 43 codes were defined; two codes used in Table 2 and the text (Skeptical, Microdosing) are not defined in Table 1, and the PHQ-9 correlations given in the text are not in Table 2 (see reporting issues). The authors state that they report all details because the project is exploratory.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the sample size is justified by published saturation estimates, not by an assessment of saturation in these data.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Hope came up in 20 of 30 stories (18 with reasonable positive hopes, 2 alluding to little hope); stories asked about side effects (19), the rationale for the treatment (15), the shortcomings of other treatments (14), subjective effects (13) and addictive potential (12); a third raised continuity of care (10). Coder-rated willingness averaged 69.5 of 100 and familiarity 40.08. Therapist abuse was mentioned in 1 story, microdosing and sitters in 4 each; 4 stories stated clearly wrong information about the treatment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and most of the discussion stay close to these counts. Two statements go beyond them: the closing sentence says the results suggest that targeted information can increase veterans' understanding, although no information was given or tested and although the Discussion had concluded that targeted information seems less necessary than brief, broad psychoeducation (p. 6, 3rd paragraph; p. 8), and the Discussion states that the FDA's 2024 rejection 'explicitly cited weaknesses in safety documentation and reporting of adverse events' with no source (p. 6). The vignette itself opens with a research project suggesting that MDMA helps, and one prompt asks about hopes; the authors acknowledge that the prompts may have created a demand for hope or optimism. The Discussion also recommends materials that emphasize that the treatment helped people with PTSD who did not respond to other interventions (p. 7, 5th paragraph), an efficacy statement without a citation.

timeline.event: MAPP1 (Mitchell et al., 2021), cited in the Introduction for a between-group effect size of d = 0.91.
MAPP2 (Mitchell et al., 2023), cited for d = 0.70 and for a more diverse sample.

FDA advisory committee meeting and rejection of the application, described in the Introduction from news reports (Jacobs, 2024; Jarow, 2024a, 2024b) and a JAMA piece (Marks, 2024), none read for this card.
This study (received January 2025; published online October 2025).

replication.where_it_stands: A first exploratory study at one site. The authors propose a survey built from these themes, in larger and more diverse samples, as the next step.

funding.funder: The authors report no funding for this work; it used resources and facilities of the Samuel S. Stratton VA Medical Center, Albany, New York.
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.
funding.affiliations_note: Mitch Earleywine: University at Albany, SUNY; Caitlin Holley and Stacey Farmer: Albany Stratton VA Medical Center; Henry MacConnel: Mount Sinai Hospital, New York. The interviewer (CH) works at the VA medical center where the participants receive care; the paper does not describe her relationship to the participants. Earleywine's earlier studies of the credibility of psychedelic and ketamine treatments are cited (Earleywine, Altman and De Leo, 2022; Low and Earleywine, 2022, 2024; Kamilar-Britt, Gordis and Earleywine, 2023).

what_would_settle_it: For how common these concerns are: a survey of a large, diverse sample of veterans with PTSD, recruited by a stated method, with items built from these themes. For the background statements on the trials and the FDA: the trial reports and the FDA's own documents, not this paper.

domains.domain: Research design appropriate to the question (qualitative appraisal, CASP-style)
domains.note: Indirect story completion suits an exploration of attitudes that people may not state about themselves; the vignette and prompts are printed in full.
One VA site; recruitment and refusals unreported; almost all White and mostly men; saturation asserted from the literature rather than assessed.

Recorded and transcribed; but the vignette opens with a favourable research finding and one prompt asks about hopes, which the authors acknowledge may create a demand for optimism; in trying to avoid stereotypes, the vignette did not emphasize the blissful side of the subjective effects.

The interviewer works at the hospital where the participants receive care and helped generate the codes; no reflexive account of interviewer or coders' views, although the first author has published on the credibility of psychedelic treatments.
IRB approval at the Stratton VA Medical Center and informed consent; data shared on request under VA policy.

Several coders with kappa reported (0.65 to 1.00) and four codes below conventional reliability kept; many correlations with no p-values or correction; codes missing from Table 1; text and tables disagree in places; codes are declared orthogonal because chi-square tests gave no p < .001 (p. 3), an unusual criterion among many tests, and Table 2 shows no code-code correlations to support the Discussion's statement that the codes did not correlate with one another.
Frequencies and an example quotation for each theme; but the inconsistencies between text and tables, and the closing inference about targeted information, are not grounded in the data.
The authors state the limits plainly: one BIPOC participant, possibly more articulate or open veterans, civilians may differ.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised as a qualitative study with the editors' qualitative checklist (METHODS §5.3). The design suits the question and the authors are candid about its limits, but recruitment is undescribed, the vignette and prompts lean toward hope, and the reporting of codes and correlations is inconsistent. The paper may be cited for which concerns these 30 veterans voiced (side effects, rationale, addictive potential, continuity of care) and how rarely therapist misconduct came up; it is not evidence on how common those concerns are, and its statements about the trials and the FDA decision are second-hand background (news reports) or unreferenced, to be cited, if at all, only as what this paper says.

key_findings.finding: Thirty veteran patients took part (25 men, 5 women; 29 White, 1 of African descent), aged 30-77 (mean 51.03, SD 14.49); all reported a previous diagnosis of, and treatment for, PTSD. Education: some college 14, college graduate 10, graduate degree 4, some high school 1, high school diploma 1.
PCL-5 scores ranged 19-65 (mean 43.67, SD 10.91); 26 of 30 were above the 31-33 range recommended for intervention; alpha 0.86. PHQ-9 ranged 8-21 (mean 14.70, SD 3.74), with alpha 0.53.
key_findings.locator: Measures › PTSD symptom severity; Depressive symptom severity (left column)

key_findings.finding: Coding produced 43 codes, of which 4 did not reach conventional reliability; Cohen's kappa ranged 0.65 to 1.00. Twenty-seven themes appeared in at least 3 of the 30 stories. Only one participant mentioned therapist abuse; four mentioned microdosing and four sitters.

Frequencies of the commonest codes: hope 20 (67%), side effects 19 (63%), rationale for the treatment 15 (50%), shortcomings of other treatments 14 (46%), subjective effects 13 (43%), addictive potential 12 (40%), continuity of care 10 (33%), impact on psychosocial function 9 (30%), difficulty of the experience 9 (30%); retraumatization 6 (20%); stigma 7 (23%); wrong information 4 (13%); concern about drug tests 4 (13%); access to VA services 3 (10%).
key_findings.note: Hope's 20 (67%) counts 18 stories with reasonable positive hopes and 2 that allude to having little hope (Table 1's definition).

key_findings.finding: Coder-rated willingness to try the treatment ranged 15-100 (mean 69.5, SD 21.21) and familiarity with it 0-90 (mean 40.08, SD 28.73); the two correlated at 0.431 (Kendall's tau).
key_findings.locator: Results › Codes (p. 3, right column, continued on p. 5, left column); Results › Covariation (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Correlations above |0.30| (Table 2): longer stories more often mentioned booster sessions (0.499), ongoing maintenance (0.468), triggering of drug problems (0.451) and shortcomings of other treatments (0.405); willingness correlated with retraumatization -0.425 and with skepticism -0.699; familiarity with skepticism -0.376 and with side effects -0.384; PCL-5 with the view that veterans are reluctant to try new treatments 0.344. No p-values are given.
Background statement about the phase 3 trials: in MAPP1 and MAPP2, MDMA-AT produced large between-group effect sizes on CAPS-5 (d = 0.91 and d = 0.70), citing Mitchell et al. (2021, 2023).
key_findings.note: Second-hand; to be checked against the trial reports (other first reader). The reference list gives volume, issue and pages for both trials that differ from Crossref (reporting issue 5).

key_findings.finding: Background statement about the FDA: the FDA rejected the application (Marks, 2024) after a split vote of an independent advisory committee, whose concerns, as reported by news sources (Jacobs, 2024; Jarow, 2024a, 2024b), included maintaining the blind given MDMA's psychoactive effects, whether the long-term safety data were sufficient, ethical concerns about therapist behaviour during trials, the difficulty of separating the effects of MDMA from the accompanying psychotherapy, and generalizability given the homogeneity of the samples.
key_findings.note: Second-hand, from news reports and a JAMA piece; no vote counts are given.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion states that the FDA's 2024 rejection of the new drug application explicitly cited weaknesses in safety documentation and in the reporting of adverse events; no source is given for this statement.

Misconceptions in the stories: at least one veteran seemed to confuse the duration of MDMA's effects with ketamine's, one questioned how an illicit drug could work as a prescription, one believed MDMA would remove the need to discuss traumatic events, and one thought the treatment required self-injection.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the stimuli may create demands despite the indirect method; the vignette did not emphasize the blissful side of the subjective effects; the prompt about hopes may create a demand for optimism; one BIPOC participant; more articulate or open veterans may be overrepresented; civilians may differ.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs (right column; the 9th continues on p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests: no funding; work supported with resources and facilities of the Samuel S. Stratton VA Medical Center; no potential conflict of interest reported.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 defines 27 themes and the two ratings, although 43 codes are reported; two codes that appear in Table 2 and in the text, 'Skeptical' and 'Microdosing', are not defined in Table 1, although microdosing was mentioned by 4 participants, above the threshold of 3 used for themes. Table 1's note says that capitalized codes are those in Table 2, but Table 2 also lists codes not capitalized in Table 1 (for example Side Effects, Neophobic, Difficulty).
reporting_issues.consequence: The full code list cannot be reconstructed; the counts of themes and codes do not reconcile.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says lifetime drug use increased with 'Wrong Information' (0.339) and 'Microdosing' (0.313), but Table 2 places 0.339 for Wrong Information under current (past-year) drug use and 0.313 for Microdosing under lifetime use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text and table disagree on which drug-use measure correlated with wrong information.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports correlations of PHQ-9 depression scores with 'Neophobic' (0.315), 'Retrauma' (0.356) and 'Hope' (0.427), but Table 2, headed as listing all correlations above |0.30| among codes and key variables, has no PHQ-9 column and no row for Hope. The Discussion also lists treatment-outcome research among the codes linked to story length, while Table 2's word-count column has ongoing maintenance but no outcome-rate code.
reporting_issues.consequence: Correlations given only in the text cannot be checked against the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Rater agreement for the willingness and familiarity ratings is given as Kendall's tau 0.76 and 0.77 in Coding, and as kappa above 0.75 in Results; percentages in Table 1 are rounded inconsistently (14 of 30 printed as 46% and 8 of 30 as 26%, but 20 of 30 as 67% and 5 of 30 as 17%; editors' calculation: 46.7%, 26.7%, 66.7%, 16.7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages should be recomputed from the counts if cited.

reporting_issues.issue: In the reference list, MAPP1 is given as Nature Medicine 27 (5):720-28 and MAPP2 as 29 (9):2020-29 with 'double-blind' in its title; the Crossref records used by this project give 27(6):1025-1033 and 29(10):2473-2480, and MAPP2's title as 'a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial'. The author lists also differ from Crossref's (Doblin is listed third for MAPP1; Lake and Sherwood appear among MAPP2's authors).
reporting_issues.consequence: The trial effect sizes quoted (d = 0.91 and 0.70) should be taken from the trial reports, not from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes 'a review of 10 trials' showing pre/post differences and lower dropout (Tedesco et al., 2021), but the reference listed under that name is a preliminary discourse analysis of therapeutic change in MDMA-assisted psychotherapy.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement is not supported by the reference as listed; not to be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the FDA's rejection explicitly cited weaknesses in safety documentation and adverse-event reporting has no source; the FDA's decision letter is not cited, and the sources given for the advisory committee are news reports.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cannot be used as evidence of the FDA's reasons; the regulator's documents are needed.

reporting_issues.issue: Two further background statements carry no citation: that the FDA granted MDMA-AT breakthrough status in 2017 (p. 1, Introduction, 2nd paragraph) and that the treatment helped people with PTSD who did not respond to other interventions (p. 7, Discussion, 5th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither is citable from this paper.
